implementerProof.how: All six items of the architect's round-thirteen scope hold, and I drove each rather than reading the handoff for it. The two counts are the round's own evidence and I ran them myself: both tests pass -count=100 with 0 failures, and the claudebridge package passes inside the loaded full suite, which is where last round's failure actually surfaced. I did not stop at those three greens: I reverted the ordering wait and watched the race return at 6 in 100, and I reverted two separate pieces of the production rule to confirm the new test bites on each half it claims. One correction to my own round-twelve record is below, in failures' place: the -race evidence I reported last round was void.

proof.criterion: Item 1 - the test sends the delivery itself, waits for the bridge's 'waits for the next step' log line, then lets the step fail; the fake that both delivered and failed is gone.
proof.surface: The claude-bridge's own process pair: the real bridge binary loop against the fake Claude Code the package starts, with a real unix inbox socket and an httptest daemon taking the turn-outcome reports.
proof.command: git diff 2e468e4b dacfc72a over bridge_test.go and turnoutcome_test.go, then cd packages/daemon && go test ./internal/claudebridge/ -count=100 -timeout 25m -run 'TestOnlyTheStepsTheProviderRefusedAreReportedRefused' | grep -c '^--- FAIL'.
proof.observed: 0 failures in 100 runs (the package line reads ok ... 4.632s, and the grep prints 0); the same command printed 19 at the previous head. The fake's fail-then case is gone, replaced by fail-when <name>, which holds the refusal at a gate; its comment now records why the fake cannot order this itself. The test dials the inbox, prompts, waits for agent_start, delivers ev1, waits for the bridge's own log line 'Envoy delivery ev1 waits for the next step', and only then releases the gate. The ordering is the test's and no longer a race.
proof.negativeControl: In a scratch clone at dacfc72a I removed the one line r.logged("Envoy delivery ev1 waits for the next step") and ran the same 100: 6 failures. So the wait is what makes the count 0, and the test still reaches the losing order when the ordering is taken away. The rate is lower than round twelve's 19 because the gate's own round trip leaves the delivery more time, which is why the control is read as non-zero against zero rather than as a rate.

proof.criterion: Item 2 - a second test covers the other order: a refusal with nothing queued is reported refused, and the delivery after it starts a new turn whose clean result clears the run.
proof.command: cd packages/daemon && go test ./internal/claudebridge/ -count=100 -timeout 25m -run 'TestARefusalWithNothingQueuedEndsItsTurnAndTheNextDeliveryIsANewOne'; then the two controls below.
proof.observed: 0 failures in 100 runs (ok ... 3.790s). TestARefusalWithNothingQueuedEndsItsTurnAndTheNextDeliveryIsANewOne prompts a refusal with nothing delivered, asserts turn 1 refused with the provider's words, then delivers ev1 and asserts turn 2 clean and the inbox answered ev1 taken. Both halves of the architect's decision are therefore pinned: the refused turn is reported as it ended, and the later delivery is a turn of its own rather than a continuation.
proof.negativeControl: Two, because the test claims two things and one control would have proved only one. First, providerRefused forced to return false: this test fails at turnoutcome_test.go:171, its refused assertion, while TestOnlyTheStepsTheProviderRefusedAreReportedRefused correctly passes, since that one wants the turn clean - so the two tests discriminate rather than overlap. Second, the turn left open (b.inRun no longer cleared when the turn ends): this test fails at turnoutcome_test.go:175, 'the bridge wrote nothing within 10s', because the delivery is then queued behind the open turn instead of starting one. The second control is the one that proves the new-turn half, which the first does not reach.

proof.criterion: Item 3 - the rule is written at bridge.go:608-611, including a delivery still in flight.
proof.observed: Nine comment lines added above result. They say which turn a delivery belongs to is decided by the queue as the result reads it and by nothing else; that a delivery already queued is the next step of this turn, one arriving after the result starts a turn of its own; and, named explicitly, that a delivery in flight - written to the inbox and not yet taken from the loop's channel - is the second case deliberately, because waiting would hold every refused turn open for as long as the inbox might still speak. That is the gap I reported last round, written down as the decision rather than left to the reader.
proof.negativeControl: The two reverts above are this item's control as well: they show the comment describes what the code does, since removing either piece of the behaviour the comment claims turns a test red.

proof.criterion: A correction to my own round-twelve evidence, which a later reader would otherwise carry forward as fact.
proof.command: go test -race ./internal/claudebridge/ -count=10 ... as I ran it in round twelve, and CGO_ENABLED=1 go test -race ./internal/claudebridge/ -count=20 -run '<test1>|<test2>' now.
proof.observed: In round twelve I reported '-race finds nothing' in the handoff, the PR body and my message to the architect. That was wrong: this pod builds with cgo off, so the command exits immediately with 'go: -race requires cgo; enable cgo by setting CGO_ENABLED=1' and runs no test at all. My grep for DATA RACE matched nothing and I read an empty result as a clean one - the same mistake in kind as reading a silently skipping suite as a passing one, which I have now made twice in different clothes. Run properly with CGO_ENABLED=1, both tests are race-clean over 20 runs each, so the conclusion stands and only its evidence was void. The round-twelve defect never depended on it: it rested on the 19-in-100 count.
proof.negativeControl: Running the bare -race command again here reproduces the refusal line verbatim, which is what shows the earlier evidence was absence of a run rather than absence of a race.

notesForNextRound: No TypeScript suite was run this round and that is deliberate: the change touches four files, three of them Go test files and one a Go comment, so no TS file is reachable from it. CI's TS lanes are the read. If a later round touches TS again, run pi-legion file by file and read each file's skip count, never its pass count; the gates are LEGION_TEST_OMP, LEGION_TEST_NATS_URL and LEGION_TEST_CLAUDE.

Use CGO_ENABLED=1 for any -race run in this pod. Without it the command exits with 'go: -race requires cgo' and runs nothing, and a grep for DATA RACE then returns the same empty output a clean run would. Read the command's own last line, not the grep's.

Start NATS before the suite, and build a database legion_test owns (psql -tAc 'create database <name> owner legion_test') rather than pointing tests at the pod DSN's postgres database, where internal/daemon's migrations fail at 0001_init with 'permission denied for schema public'.
